Among the exam's four options, more than one is defensible: option (a) is the clearly correct, substantive statement, but option (d) ("is present in adipose tissue") is also technically true, if trivial/circular. evidence: Primary polycythemia (vera) “is usually accompanied with increased production of WBCs and platelets” and secondary polycythemia “occurs when tissues become hypoxic… at high altitudes” (both a and c true); viscosity increase (b) is confirmed on p.136. The book never attributes polycythemia directly to “excessive secretion of erythropoietin,” making D the best-supported exception by elimination — but this option is also defensible as true in general medicine (EPO-secreting tumours cause secondary polycythemia), which is the source of the doubt flagged below.
reviewNote: Question 14 (polycythemia). The book confirms that primary polycythemia (polycythemia vera) is usually accompanied by increased WBC and platelet production, that it increases blood viscosity, and that secondary polycythemia occurs at high altitude — so options A, B and C are all true per the text, leaving D (“can result from excessive secretion of erythropoietin hormone”) as the best-supported exception by elimination. However, D is also a defensible TRUE statement in general medicine, since secondary polycythemia can genuinely result from an EPO-secreting tumor (e.g. renal cell carcinoma) or from exogenous EPO — the book simply does not frame secondary polycythemia in EPO terms. This creates a real risk that more than one option is defensible as the intended “except,” depending on whether “polycythemia” in the stem is read as polycythemia vera specifically (EPO-independent, favouring D as the exception) or polycythemia in general (where D would actually be true). Faculty should confirm the intended scope of the question before this is auto-scored.

text: During well fed state, which of the following metabolic changes occurs in carbohydrate metabolism in the liver?
sourceExam: Module 103 — End-of-Module Examination — Batch 198 — Academic Year 2024-2025
textbookEdition: BMS 103 — Biomedical Sciences & Musculoskeletal Sciences, Academic Year 2026-2027 (Faculty of Medicine, Cairo University). Biochemistry questions are additionally cross-checked against Dr. Hisham Esmat's Biochemistry book, prepared for Batch 199, academic year 2025–2026, where the department book has no usable text for this academic year.
evidence: the book confirms the actual well-fed-state direction of each process is the opposite of what the options state: insulin “activates glycogen synthase and inactivates glycogen phosphorylase” (page 45 — glycogenolysis falls, not rises as option A says); insulin stimulates “Dehydrogenases of HMP: providing NADPH” (page 65 — HMP activity rises, not falls as option B says); in the fed state “Insulin decreases the activity of gluconeogenic key enzymes” (page 52 — gluconeogenesis falls, not rises as option C says); and insulin “increases activity of glycolytic key enzymes” (page 52 — glycolysis rises, not falls as option D says).
reviewNote: As literally worded, none of the four options describes an actual well-fed-state change in hepatic carbohydrate metabolism: (A) glycogenolysis decreases (not increases) when fed; (B) HMP-shunt activity increases (not decreases), providing NADPH for lipogenesis; (C) gluconeogenesis decreases (not increases) when fed; (D) glycolysis increases (not decreases) when fed. The item most plausibly has a wording/typing error (e.g. "increase" and "decrease" transposed on one or more options, most likely intended as "increase glycogenesis" for option A or "increase HMP activity" for option B); as supplied, no option is defensible. This conclusion has been independently checked against Dr. Hisham Esmat's Biochemistry book (printed pages 45, 52 and 65), which confirms the actual fed-state direction of every one of the four processes is the opposite of what its corresponding option states, so no option is defensible even against this second source.
